talktitle: Compact oracles for reachability and approximate distances in planar digraphs
abstract: It is shown that a planar digraph can be preprocessed in near-linear time, producing a near-linear space oracle that can answer reachability queries in constant time. The oracle can be distributed as an O(log n) space label for each vertex and then we can determine if one vertex can reach another considering their two labels only.The approach generalizes to give a near-linear space approximate distances oracle for a weighted planar digraph. With weights drawn from {0, …, N}, it approximates distances within a factor (1 + ε) in O(log log (nN) + 1/ε) time. Our scheme can be extended to find and route along correspondingly short dipaths.

Speaker: Ho-Lin Chen
title: Professor
expertise: Algorithm Design, Molecular Computing, Algorithmic Game Theory
talktitle: Self-Stabilizing Leader Election in Population Protocols
abstract:
Population protocols provide a simple model of distributed computation in which anonymous agents with limited memory interact in pairs to perform collective tasks. Leader election is one of the fundamental problems in this model. In the self-stabilizing variant, the protocol must converge to a configuration with a unique leader from any initial configuration and maintain this property thereafter. Despite its simple formulation, self-stabilizing leader election presents significant challenges, particularly when the agents have limited memory or the network size is unknown.

In this talk, I will present a series of results on self-stabilizing leader election in population protocols. We first show that a constant number of states suffices to solve the problem on rings of arbitrary sizes, and extend this approach to tori and regular graphs. Although these protocols require exponential convergence time, they demonstrate that self-stabilization is possible with extremely limited memory. We then turn to complete graphs and investigate the tradeoff between stabilization time and the number of states. In particular, we obtain an asymptotically optimal linear-time protocol with a linear number of states, as well as faster protocols that achieve sublinear and even logarithmic stabilization time at the cost of substantially larger state spaces.

Finally, I will discuss several recent developments that further improve these tradeoffs, including near-time-optimal protocols with polylogarithmic and polyloglog states on rings, and new approaches that significantly reduce the state complexity of sublinear-time protocols on complete graphs.

Speaker: Peter Rossmanith
title: Professor
talktitle: When Exact Algorithms Are Elusive: What Should We Relax?
abstract:
When an exact algorithm is too expensive, the usual response is to seek a polynomial-time approximation algorithm. But a different relaxation may give a more useful guarantee. I will give several examples of how problems can be relaxed, then examine three ways to relax the problem of covering a graph with k shortest paths. 

We can keep k shortest paths and cover almost all vertices; cover every vertex while allowing up to 2k shortest paths; or keep k paths and full coverage while allowing each subpath to be at most 1 + ε times as long as a shortest path. Each version admits a fixed-parameter algorithm that succeeds whenever an exact k-path cover exists. These results show how the choice of what to relax can matter as much as the algorithm itself.

Speaker: Marcus Wilhelm
title: Postdoc Researcher
expertise: Graph Algorithms, Parameterized Complexity, Randomized Analysis, Geometry
talktitle: Diameter Computation Between Theory and Practice
abstract:
The diameter of a graph is defined as the maximum distance between any two vertices. Despite being a fundamental graph problem with many applications, there remains a large gap between well-understood theoretical algorithms and the approaches used for diameter computation in practice.

In this talk we consider the iterative fringe upper bound (iFUB) by Crescenzi et al., and gain an intuition for its good performance on real-world networks with the exception of torus-like geometric graphs. To overcome this limitation, we develop a new algorithm with provable performance guarantees on (torus) random geometric graphs. Finally, we explore results from  engineering an efficient implementation of this algorithm and see how well it performs in practice.
